usage: 사업하다 is also one verb; once you add the object marker 을 you must split it: 사업을 하다
시작하다 = to begin; 사업을 차리다 (to set up a business) is a more colloquial alternative
잘되다 is one word and intransitive; the opposite is 사업이 안되다 (business is doing badly)
계획 = plan; 사업 모델, 사업 분야, 사업 자금 also use 사업 as a bare modifier (no 의)
examples: 저는 작은 사업을 하고 싶어요.
I want to run a small business.
Beginner frame: 사업을 하다 split by 을; 작은 modifies 사업
요즘 경기가 안 좋아서 사업이 잘 안돼요.
Business isn't going well these days because the economy is bad.
안돼요 = isn't going well; -아서 gives the reason and can't take a past tense before it
그분은 맨손으로 시작해서 사업으로 크게 성공한 분이에요.
He started from nothing and made it big in business.
사업으로 = through/in business; 맨손으로 = with bare hands, a real-life success-story phrase
nuance: 사업 (事業, literally 'affair-work') is business as an active undertaking — running a company, launching a commercial project, or being self-employed. The key boundary is against 산업 (産業, industry as a whole sector): 사업 is what one person or firm concretely does, while 산업 is the field that many businesses belong to (자동차 산업 = the auto industry, but 자동차 사업 = a particular auto-related business venture). It is also broader than the English word — a government or non-profit project is a 사업 too (복지 사업 = welfare project), so don't restrict it to 'for-profit'. Register is neutral; everyone from a small shop owner to a CEO uses it. The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 사업하다 as a fixed block: the moment an object marker appears you must break it apart (사업을 하다, 사업을 시작하다), never 사업하다를. Also resist translating 'do business with someone' word-for-word — Koreans say 거래하다 (to trade/deal) for that, not 사업을 하다.

'Do business with a partner' is not 그 사람과 사업을 하다 — Koreans say 그 사람과 거래하다 (to deal/trade with) for an ongoing commercial relationship.

usage: 산업 follows the field as a bare modifier: 반도체 산업, 관광 산업, 게임 산업
발전하다 = to develop/advance; 산업이 성장하다 (to grow) is an equally common partner
구조 = structure; describes how an economy's sectors are organized and is heavy news/policy vocabulary
첨단 = cutting-edge; the natural contrast is 전통 산업 (traditional industry) or 사양 산업 (declining industry)
examples: 한국은 반도체 산업이 발달해 있어요.
Korea's semiconductor industry is well developed.
Beginner frame: 발달해 있다 = is in a developed state; V-아/어 있다 marks a resulting condition
인공지능 관련 산업이 빠르게 성장하고 있어요.
AI-related industries are growing fast.
관련 = related (attached directly, no 의); -고 있다 here marks an ongoing change/trend
이 지역은 한때 조선 산업으로 먹고살았지만 지금은 관광에 의존해요.
This region once lived off the shipbuilding industry but now depends on tourism.
(으)로 먹고살다 = to make a living off; 의존하다 = to depend on — a real regional-economy sentence
nuance: 산업 (産業, 'produce-work') is an industry as an entire economic sector — manufacturing, tourism, IT — never a single company. Use it for macro-level talk: news, government reports, and any discussion of how the economy is structured. The sharp dividing line is against 사업 (事業, business venture): many 사업체 (businesses) together make up one 산업. So 산업을 시작하다 is wrong for 'start a business' — a person cannot launch a whole sector; they start a 사업. A related near-synonym is 업종 (業種, line of business / business category), but 업종 is narrower and is used to classify an individual shop ('what 업종 is your store?'), whereas 산업 is the broad sector above it. Register is formal-to-neutral; you will rarely hear 산업 in casual chat about your own job, but constantly in writing. The English-speaker pitfall is letting the romanization blur it with 사업 — the 산(ㄴ받침) vs 사 distinction is the entire meaning, and the two are not interchangeable.

Don't let the similar sound merge 산업 (industry) and 사업 (business): the ㄴ batchim in 산 carries the entire meaning difference.
To say what field a small shop is in, Koreans usually ask 업종이 뭐예요? (what's the line of business?), not 산업이 뭐예요? — 산업 is too macro for one store.

usage: the opposite is 경력이 없다; this is a track record, not a one-off experience
쌓다 = to pile up/accumulate — the idiomatic verb; 경력을 만들다 sounds wrong
number + 년 directly after 경력 states length; 경력 단절 = a career gap/break
-직 = position/post; the contrast term in hiring is 신입 (new-graduate hire)
examples: 저는 경력이 별로 없어요.
I don't really have much (work) experience.
Beginner frame: 경력이 없다; 별로 + negative = not really/much
마케팅 분야에서 경력을 더 쌓고 싶어요.
I want to build up more experience in the marketing field.
분야에서 = in the field of; 쌓다 is the fixed verb for accumulating a career
경력이 화려해도 인성이 안 좋으면 뽑지 않아요.
Even with a dazzling résumé, we don't hire someone with poor character.
경력이 화려하다 = to have an impressive career; -아도 = even if — a real hiring-panel remark
nuance: 경력 (經歷, 'pass-through + experience', i.e. things you have lived/worked through) means accumulated professional experience or work history — exactly what fills the career section of a résumé. The critical contrast is with 경험 (經驗): 경험 is experience of any kind, including a fun trip, a first kiss, or eating something new, whereas 경력 is specifically a documented work/professional track record. A backpacking trip is a great 경험 but is not 경력; three years at a company is both. Because it is a record, 경력 is counted in years with 년 (경력 3년), not with 번 (times) or 개 (items). High-frequency offshoots dominate Korean hiring: 경력직 (experienced hire) versus 신입 (new graduate), and 경력 단절 (a career break, often used for women returning to work). Register is neutral and shows up on every job posting. The English-speaker pitfall is using 경력 wherever English says 'experience' — for the broad sense ('It was a great experience'), you need 경험, and swapping them sounds odd to a Korean ear.

usage: 채용하다 is what the company does; the agent is the employer, not the applicant
공고 = public notice; the place openings are announced (채용 공고를 보다 = to see a job ad)
신입 = entry-level; the partner term is 경력 채용 (experienced-hire recruitment)
과정 = process; 채용이 되다 = to get hired (passive); 채용을 취소하다 = to cancel a hire
examples: 그 회사는 올해 신입을 많이 채용해요.
That company is hiring a lot of new graduates this year.
Beginner frame: 신입을 채용하다 — the company is the subject
채용 공고를 보고 지원서를 냈어요.
I saw the job posting and submitted my application.
-고 = and then; 지원서를 내다 = to hand in an application — note the applicant 지원한다, not 채용한다
요즘은 수시 채용이 늘어서 공채 시즌이 거의 사라졌어요.
Open-ended hiring has grown lately, so the mass-recruitment season has nearly vanished.
수시 채용 = rolling/as-needed hiring vs 공채 (公採, scheduled mass recruitment) — current job-market vocabulary
nuance: 채용 (採用, 'pick/gather + use', i.e. to select and put to use) is the formal, institutional word for recruitment and hiring that companies use — it dominates 채용 공고 (job postings) and 채용 과정 (the hiring process). The register contrast is against the everyday verb 뽑다 (to pick/select): a friend might casually say 회사에서 사람 뽑는대 (I hear the company is taking people on), but the official notice says 채용. The directional pitfall trips up English speakers constantly: the employer 채용한다 (hires/recruits), while the applicant 지원한다 (applies) — these are not interchangeable, so '저는 그 회사에 채용했어요' to mean 'I applied' is wrong; you 지원했어요 and were then 채용됐어요 (got hired). Note also that 입사하다 (to enter a company, already in vocab) is the later step of actually joining after the offer. Spelling matters: the first syllable is 채 (ㅐ), not 체. Worth knowing the modern split: 공채 (scheduled mass hiring) versus 수시 채용 (rolling hiring), a frequent news topic.

Don't write 채용 as 체용 — the first syllable is 채 (ㅐ).
Getting hired is the passive 채용되다 (저는 채용됐어요), not the active 채용하다, which would mean you did the hiring.

usage: the opposite is 수입이 적다; describes how much money comes in
줄다 = to decrease (intransitive); 수입이 늘다 = income increases
한 달 = one month; 고정 수입 = fixed/steady income, 부수입 = side income
지출 (already in vocab) = outgo; this is the standard budgeting pair (in vs out)
examples: 저는 한 달 수입이 많지 않아요.
My monthly income isn't very high.
Beginner frame: 수입이 많다/적다; 많지 않다 = not much
프리랜서는 매달 수입이 일정하지 않아서 불안해요.
A freelancer's income isn't steady month to month, so it's stressful.
일정하다 = to be steady/fixed; -지 않아서 chains the negative reason
수입보다 지출이 많으면 적자가 나니까 가계부를 써 보세요.
If spending exceeds income you run a deficit, so try keeping a budget book.
적자가 나다 = to go into the red; N보다 = than — a practical money-management line
nuance: 수입 for personal money means income or revenue — the money coming in — and lives in opposition to 지출 (spending going out). Crucially it is a homograph hiding two different hanja: 收入 ('gather + enter') is income, while 輸入 ('transport + enter') is imports, the opposite of 수출 (輸出, exports). Spoken aloud they are identical, so only context tells you whether 수입 means a paycheck or a shipment of foreign goods; in an economics lecture both senses can appear in one paragraph. The near-synonym for the income sense is 소득 (所得, already in vocab): 소득 is the more formal/statistical word (소득세 = income tax, 소득 수준 = income level), whereas 수입 feels closer to everyday earnings, especially 한 달 수입 (monthly take). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 'income' maps only to one fixed word and then panicking when 수입 shows up meaning 'imports' — train yourself to read the surrounding sentence. Also note 수입 is a noun describing a state (수입이 많다), so you don't conjugate it like a verb.

usage: 보다 here means 'to incur', not 'to see' — the single most important collocation to memorize
입다 = to suffer (slightly more formal); 손해를 끼치다 = to cause a loss to someone else
크다/적다 size the loss; 손해가 막심하다 = the loss is severe (set phrase)
배상 = indemnity; 손해 배상을 청구하다 = to claim damages — legal/business register
examples: 그렇게 하면 제가 손해예요.
If we do it that way, I lose out.
Beginner frame: noun-as-predicate 손해(이)다 = to be a loss/disadvantage to someone
지금 팔면 손해를 볼 것 같아서 조금 더 기다리려고요.
I think I'll take a loss if I sell now, so I'll wait a bit longer.
손해를 보다 = to incur a loss; -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 = it seems — note 보다 is NOT 'see' here
환불을 안 해 주면 결국 소비자만 손해를 보는 거잖아요.
If they won't refund it, in the end it's only the consumer who loses out, right?
결국 = in the end; -잖아요 = appeals to shared knowledge — a real complaint-line
nuance: 손해 (損害, 'damage + harm') is a loss or disadvantage, almost always financial or in terms of coming out worse off — the direct opposite of 이익/이득 (profit/gain). Its make-or-break collocation is 손해를 보다, where 보다 does NOT mean 'to see' but 'to incur/take', so 손해를 보다 = 'to take a loss'; English speakers often mis-hear this and either mistranslate it or wrongly substitute 손해를 하다, which is simply not Korean. The boundary against 피해 (被害, harm/damage suffered) matters: 손해 leans toward monetary or deal-based disadvantage (a bad sale, an unfair trade), while 피해 covers broader harm including physical or disaster damage (태풍 피해 = typhoon damage, 피해자 = victim). For a machine breaking, use 고장 (malfunction), not 손해. Register is neutral and it even works conversationally as a predicate noun: 나만 손해야 (I'm the only one who loses out). The pitfall to drill is the verb pairing — 손해를 보다 / 입다, never 손해를 하다.

손해 is monetary/disadvantage loss; for broad harm — physical, disaster, victim — use 피해 (태풍 피해, 피해자), and for a device breaking use 고장.
손해 is the opposite of 이익 (profit), so don't mix it up with 손님 (guest/customer), which only looks similar.

usage: the opposite is 가치가 없다 (worthless); covers both economic and abstract worth
오르다/떨어지다 for value going up/down (property, stocks, currency, a collectible)
예: 볼 가치가 있다 (worth seeing), 도전해 볼 가치가 있다 (worth trying)
-관 (觀) = view; 가치관이 다르다 = to have different values — a very common relationship phrase
examples: 이건 정말 가치가 있어요.
This really has value / is worthwhile.
Beginner frame: 가치가 있다 as a simple predicate of worth
그 그림은 시간이 지날수록 가치가 올라갔어요.
That painting rose in value as time went by.
-(으)ㄹ수록 = the more...; 가치가 오르다/올라가다 for appreciating value
저는 일을 고를 때 연봉보다 그 일의 가치를 더 중요하게 봐요.
When I pick a job, I weigh the meaning of the work over the salary.
고를 때 = when choosing; 중요하게 보다 = to regard as important — a real values-based statement
nuance: 가치 (價値, 'price + value') means value or worth, spanning both economic value (가치가 오르다 = rises in value, of property or stocks) and abstract worth (인생의 가치 = the value of life, 일의 가치 = the worth of one's work). The most useful pattern built on it is V-(으)ㄹ 가치가 있다 ('worth doing': 볼 가치가 있다 = worth seeing), and the derived 가치관 (one's value system/worldview) is extremely high-frequency, especially 가치관이 다르다 when people clash. The dividing line is against the concrete-amount words 가격 (價格, the listed price/price tag) and 값 (the cost/amount you actually pay): 가치 is how much something is truly worth, which may diverge sharply from its 가격 — a cheap gift can have huge 가치 but a low 가격. Register is neutral-to-elevated. The English-speaker pitfall is forcing 가치 into the 'worth doing' slot with the wrong verb (가치가 하다 is wrong; it's 가치가 있다), and mixing it up with 가격 when you mean the sticker price rather than intrinsic worth.

The pitfall is forcing 가치 into the 'worth doing' slot with the wrong verb (가치가 하다 is wrong; it's 가치가 있다), and mixing it up with 가격 when you mean the sticker price rather than intrinsic worth.

mistakes: Don't confuse 가치 (intrinsic worth/value) with 가격 (the listed price): a discounted item has a low 가격 but can still hold high 가치.
For 'worth doing' use V-(으)ㄹ 가치가 있다 (볼 가치가 있다), never 가치가 하다.
To say people have clashing values, the idiom is 가치관이 다르다 (different value systems), not 가치가 다르다.

usage: the negatives are 품질이 나쁘다 and 품질이 떨어지다 (quality drops/is poor)
높이다 = to raise (transitive); 품질을 관리하다 = to manage/control quality
관리 = management; a standard business term, often abbreviated 품질 관리부 (QC department)
고- (高) / 저- (低) prefixes attach directly to 품질
examples: 이 옷은 품질이 좋아요.
This clothing is good quality.
Beginner frame: 품질이 좋다 — 품질 is the subject, 좋다 the descriptive verb
가격은 조금 비싸지만 품질이 정말 좋아서 만족해요.
It's a bit pricey, but the quality is so good that I'm satisfied.
-지만 = but; -아서 chains the reason 'because the quality is good'
요즘 소비자들은 가격보다 품질을 더 꼼꼼하게 따져요.
These days consumers scrutinize quality more carefully than price.
따지다 (already in vocab) = to scrutinize; 꼼꼼하게 = meticulously — a market-trend sentence
nuance: 품질 (品質, 'goods + substance/quality') refers specifically to the quality of goods or products — how well-made and reliable something is. It is THE word in commerce and reviews: 품질 관리 (quality control), 품질 보증 (quality guarantee), 품질이 떨어지다 (quality slips). The sharp restriction English speakers must learn is that 품질 only modifies products/goods, not abstract or experiential things: 'quality of life' is 삶의 질, 'quality of sleep' is 수면의 질, 'quality time' is not 품질 시간 — for all of those you drop the 품 and use bare 질 (質, quality/nature). So 품(品) literally pins it to merchandise. The near-synonym to keep separate is 성능 (性能, performance/specs of a device): a phone can have great 성능 (fast chip) but poor 품질 (cheap, breaks easily) — capability versus build quality. Register is neutral. The pitfall: 품질 is a noun naming a state, so you describe it with 좋다/나쁘다 (품질이 좋다), and you never say 품질을 잘하다, which treats it like an action.

usage: 생산하다 = to make/manufacture; the factory or firm is the agent
늘다/줄다 (intransitive) for output rising/falling; 생산을 늘리다 = to increase output (transitive)
대량 = large quantity; the contrast is 소량 생산 (small-batch) and 다품종 소량 생산 (high-mix low-volume)
라인, 과정 attach to 생산 as compounds; 생산성 = productivity
examples: 이 공장은 자동차를 생산해요.
This factory produces cars.
Beginner frame: A를 생산하다; 공장 (factory) as the natural subject
원자재 가격이 올라서 생산 비용이 늘었어요.
Production costs rose because raw-material prices went up.
원자재 = raw materials; 비용 (already in vocab) = cost — 생산 as a compound modifier
수요가 갑자기 늘면 생산을 그만큼 늘려야 하는데 공장이 못 따라가요.
If demand suddenly jumps you have to raise output to match, but the factory can't keep up.
수요 = demand; 생산을 늘리다 (transitive); 따라가다 = to keep pace — a real supply-chain bind
nuance: 생산 (生産, 'give birth/bring forth + produce') means production or manufacturing — the making of goods. It is the supply side of the economy and pairs naturally with 소비 (消費, consumption) as a set: 생산과 소비. The agent is a 생산자 (producer), the mirror of 소비자 (consumer). Keep three look-alike Sino-Korean economy words apart: 생산 (making things/output) vs 산업 (産業, the industry sector that does the making) vs 사업 (事業, a specific business venture) — they share syllables but mean output, sector, and enterprise respectively. The most common grammar pitfall is the transitivity pair English flattens into one verb 'increase': 생산이 늘다 is intransitive ('production increases', no object), but to actively raise output you need the transitive 생산을 늘리다 ('increase production'); using 생산을 늘다 is ungrammatical. Register is neutral-to-formal, standard in business and news. Note 대량 생산 (mass production) as a fixed term and 생산성 (productivity) as a high-value derivative.

Match transitivity: 생산이 늘다 (production rises, intransitive) vs 생산을 늘리다 (raise production, transitive). 생산을 늘다 is ungrammatical.
The person who produces is 생산자, not 생산가 — the agent suffix here is -자 (者), paralleling 소비자 (consumer).

usage: 소비하다 also takes 에너지를/자원을 소비하다 (consume energy/resources)
늘다/줄다 (intransitive) for spending rising or falling; 소비를 줄이다 = to cut spending (transitive)
-자 (者) = person; the mirror of 생산자 (producer); 소비자 보호 = consumer protection
과- (過) = excessive; the positive contrast is 합리적 소비 (sensible consumption)
examples: 요즘 소비를 줄이고 있어요.
I'm cutting back on spending these days.
Beginner frame: 소비를 줄이다 (transitive); -고 있다 for an ongoing effort
경기가 나빠지면 사람들이 소비를 줄여요.
When the economy worsens, people reduce their spending.
나빠지다 = to get worse; 줄이다 = to reduce — the cause–effect of a downturn
요즘 젊은 세대는 가치 소비를 중요하게 생각해서 비싸도 의미 있는 걸 사요.
Young people today value 'ethical/meaningful consumption', so they buy meaningful things even if pricey.
가치 소비 = value-driven consumption; -아도 = even if — a current consumer-culture trend
nuance: 소비 (消費, 'dissolve/use up + spend') means consumption or spending — using up money, goods, or resources — and is the demand-side counterpart to 생산 (production), giving the staple pair 생산과 소비. Its standout derivative 소비자 (consumer) is one of the most useful economy words you can own (소비자 보호 = consumer protection). Two boundaries matter. First, against 지출 (支出, expenditure, already in vocab): 지출 is an accounting outflow — a line item in a budget — while 소비 is the broader economic act of consuming, including consuming non-money resources. Second, and the key value judgment, against 낭비 (浪費, waste): 소비 is neutral and often necessary (you must consume food and electricity), whereas 낭비 is always negative — money or resources thrown away pointlessly. So calling ordinary, reasonable spending 낭비 is an insult the speaker may not intend. Register is neutral. The grammar pitfall mirrors 생산: use the transitive 소비를 줄이다 to 'reduce spending', not the intransitive 소비를 줄다.

Match transitivity: 소비를 줄이다 (cut spending, transitive) vs 소비가 줄다 (spending falls, intransitive). 소비를 줄다 is wrong.
소비 is the broad act of consuming; an individual budget outflow/expense entry is 지출 — don't use 소비 where the accounting term 지출 is meant.

usage: 짜다 = to put together/plan; the most natural verb (it's a structured plan you assemble)
부족하다 = to be short; the opposite is 예산이 남다 (budget left over)
세우다 = to set up; 예산을 초과하다 = to exceed the budget
안에서 = inside; the contrast is 예산을 넘다/초과하다 (to go over budget)
examples: 이번 여행은 예산이 좀 부족해요.
I'm a bit short on budget for this trip.
Beginner frame: 예산이 부족하다; 좀 softens it
회사에서 내년 마케팅 예산을 줄이기로 했어요.
The company decided to cut next year's marketing budget.
-기로 하다 = to decide to; 예산을 줄이다 = to reduce the budget
예산을 미리 짜 두면 충동구매를 줄일 수 있어요.
If you set a budget in advance, you can curb impulse buying.
-아/어 두다 = do in advance and leave it; 충동구매 = impulse purchase — a practical money tip
nuance: 예산 (豫算, 'beforehand + calculate', i.e. money figured out in advance) is a budget — a planned amount of money set aside for a project, household, or organization before it is spent. The idiomatic verb is 예산을 짜다 ('to weave/assemble a budget'), reflecting that a budget is a structured plan you build; 예산을 세우다 (to set up) also works, but 예산을 만들다 (to make) sounds flat and unnatural. The defining contrast is the plan-versus-actual distinction English blurs under 'budget': 예산 is the forward-looking plan, whereas 지출 (expenditure, already in vocab) and 비용 (the cost incurred) are what actually leaves your pocket, and 가계부 is the record of what was spent. So you 예산을 짜다 first, then track your 지출 against it. Register is neutral and identical in households, companies, and government (국가 예산 = the national budget). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 만들다 to 'make a budget' and confusing the planned 예산 with already-spent 지출/비용 — keep 'plan' (예산) and 'spent' (지출) firmly apart.

예산 is the planned amount looking forward, not money already spent — that is 지출 (expenditure) or 비용 (cost).
To go over budget say 예산을 초과하다/넘다, not 예산을 지나다 (which means physically pass by).

usage: 부족하다 = to lack; the classic startup problem (initial capital shortfall)
투자하다 = to invest; 자본을 모으다 = to raise/gather capital
-금 (金) = money/funds; the registered founding capital of a company
-주의 (主義) = -ism; 외국 자본 = foreign capital, 자본 시장 = capital market
examples: 사업을 하려면 자본이 필요해요.
To run a business you need capital.
Beginner frame: 자본이 필요하다; -(으)려면 = if you intend to
그들은 적은 자본으로 회사를 크게 키웠어요.
They grew the company big on little capital.
적은 = small/little; 키우다 = to grow (something) — 자본으로 = with/using capital
외국 자본이 한국 시장에 몰리면서 부동산 가격이 들썩였어요.
As foreign capital poured into the Korean market, property prices got jittery.
몰리다 = to flood/crowd in; 들썩이다 = to be unsettled — a real macroeconomic sentence
nuance: 자본 (資本, 'resources + root/origin', i.e. the foundational resources of an enterprise) is capital in the economic sense — the money and assets used to start or run a business and to generate more wealth. It is more abstract and formal than plain 돈 (money), and it carries a structural, economy-level flavor: 자본주의 (capitalism), 자본 시장 (capital market), 외국 자본 (foreign capital). Two near-synonyms must be separated. 자금 (資金, funds) is money earmarked for a specific concrete purpose — 사업 자금 (operating funds), 자금이 돌다 (cash flows) — more hands-on than the foundational 자본. And 자산 (資産, assets) is the total of what you own (property, savings, stocks), the broadest of the three. So you might have plenty of 자산 (assets) but lack ready 자금 (working funds), while 자본 names the wealth deployed to do business. The key derivative 자본금 (paid-in capital) is the registered founding sum. The English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 자본 for everyday pocket cash (that's 돈) or for purpose-specific funds (that's 자금), and don't drop the final ㄴ — it is 자본, not 자보.
